headline_en: Little Adnan gets a new life
summary_en: Very relieving news has come from a hospital in Dubai. Here, little Adnan had been undergoing a unique treatment since birth. He was suffering severe seizures every thirteen minutes. He had seizures about one hundred and ten times every day. Doctors decided to try a new experimental treatment. Adnan was given this new medicine. As soon as the medicine was given, his seizures stopped completely. This relief continued throughout the day, the whole week, and for weeks to come. The hospital team is extremely happy with this wonderful result. This discovery has become a new ray of hope for many critically ill children. Adnan's family is now breathing a sigh of relief.

lead.title: Infant Goes from 110 Seizures a Day to Seizure-Free with Experimental Treatment
lead.summary: From the first day of his life, little infant Adnan has suffered a seizure roughly every 13 minutes. One can only imagine the reactions from his Dubai hospital bedside when, having received a still-experimental drug, his seizures stopped for the day. And for the week, and the week after that—and the week after that. headline_hi: धारावी के स्कूल को बचाने की मुहिम
summary_en: New Life School in Mumbai's Dharavi has been running for the past forty years. Five hundred and sixty young children come here to study every day. This school did not have ownership rights to its land. Now, amidst Dharavi's new redevelopment, saving this land is very important. Nineteen-year-old college student Daniel Gupta took on this responsibility. Along with his friends, he started a campaign named Dharavi Rising. In the beginning, against a target of twenty lakh, they raised twenty-two lakh rupees. Now their goal is to raise one and a half crore rupees for the school's land. Daniel believes that children's education should not stop under any circumstances. This campaign is giving a new identity to the future of the entire neighborhood.

lead.title: A 40-Year-Old Dharavi School Needs Its Land. This 19-YO Is Leading the Fight
lead.summary: For 560 children at New Life School in Dharavi, Mumbai, the future of their education depends on one question: will their school continue to exist where it stands today? The preschool has been educating children in the neighbourhood for four decades. Yet, throughout its 40-year history, it has never owned the land on which it operates. Now, as Dharavi undergoes redevelopment, securing that land has become central to ensuring the school's future. An effort to help the institution do so has brought together an unlikely group: a 19-year-old college student, his friends and a community determined to preserve access to education for the neighbourhood's children.   Taking on a fundraising campaign of this scale meant Daniel had to understand several areas beyond his college curriculum, including corporate social responsibility (CSR) funding, institutional philanthropy and campaign strategy.   Daniel Gupta, a third-year advertising and media student at Mumbai University, is leading the effort through an initiative called Dharavi Rising. After raising Rs 22 lakh against an initial target of Rs 20 lakh for the school's expansion, the team has now set its sights on a much larger goal: Rs 1.5 crore to help the school secure its land and continue serving children in the neighbourhood. For Daniel, the initiative is about more than keeping a school open. It is also an attempt to change how people see Dharavi, a neighbourhood often discussed through the lens of overcrowding, poverty and redevelopment, rather than through the lives, aspirations and institutions of the people who call it home. headline_en: Ban on oil drilling in Los Angeles
summary_en: There is news of a big victory for the environment from the American city of Los Angeles. People living near oil wells there had been troubled for years. Toxic gases and methane were causing an increase in respiratory illnesses among residents. Wendy Miranda and her organization fought against this for ten years. Both Wendy and her mother were battling asthma. Now the city council has imposed a complete ban on oil drilling in the city. An immediate ban has been placed on drilling new wells. All old wells will be permanently shut down over the next twenty years. Los Angeles has become the largest city in America to take such a historic step. This decision will allow millions of people to get clean and healthy air.
source: The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News

lead.title: After a decade of community pressure, LA bans oil drilling for good
lead.summary: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM For more than a decade, residents in some of Los Angeles’s most densely populated neighborhoods have lived alongside oil wells: down the street from active drilling operations, near idle wells leaking methane, in communities where benzene and hydrogen sulfide from nearby extraction have been connected to higher rates of respiratory illness and reduced lung function. On October 28, the LA City Council voted to end that. The ordinance bans new drilling immediately, prohibits the deepening or redrilling of existing wells, and requires all active operations within city limits to phase out over the next 20 years. Los Angeles is now the largest city in the United States to ban oil extraction, and the first to kick the industry out entirely. A decade of community pressure It took more than ten years to get here, and Wendy Miranda, a policy director with Esperanza Community Housing , has been campaigning with STAND-LA , a coalition of community groups working to end neighborhood drilling, for most of that time. “Front-line communities have pushed the city for a solution for this for over a decade,” she said. For Miranda, the campaign was personal as much as political. She and her mother both have asthma , and many of the communities closest to the wells are working-class neighborhoods of color where residents have absorbed the health costs of extraction for generations. “Frontline communities have been experiencing or have experienced for decades living near these toxic sites and having to pay for that with their health,” she said. headline_en: A unique school for refugee children
summary_en: More than seventeen thousand people live in Zimbabwe's Tongogara refugee camp. In the year twenty-twenty, schools there were closed due to the lockdown. Young Prince Bashangezi and his companions did not just sit back and wait. They formed a study group named Tweens for refugee children. Older students began teaching younger children for free right inside the camp. Despite a lack of resources, these students encouraged one another. An organization named Education Matters Africa also fully supported them. This campaign became a means to keep children's education going during difficult times. This effort by Prince proves that if the resolve is strong, anything is possible. Now this group has become the foundation for a better future for the camp's children.
source: The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News

lead.title: Prince Bashangezi turned personal loss into peer tutoring for refugee students
lead.summary: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM This article is part of The Optimist Daily’s Local Changemakers 2026 series, spotlighting changemakers 30 and under. In March 2020, COVID lockdowns shuttered schools around the world, including at Tongogara Refugee Camp in Zimbabwe, where Prince Bashangezi was completing his A-Level studies. The camp sits near the Mozambique border, home to more than 17,000 people displaced by conflict across central and eastern Africa. Formal schooling stopped. Prince and a group of fellow A-Level students at USAP Community School, a school serving refugee youth in the camp, decided not to wait for it to resume. They founded TWEENS : Together We Educationally Empower Non-privileged Students. The model was built around what they had: each other. Teaching from inside the camp TWEENS began as a service learning project, with refugee students tutoring younger students in the same camp. The premise was direct. These were students who understood exactly what it meant to study without resources, without stability , often without continuous access to teachers, and in many cases without families to support them. They knew the particular difficulty of trying to build a future from inside a displaced population. So they taught each other. The program was supported by Education Matters Africa , a Zimbabwe-based nonprofit, and launched at a moment when any alternative to organized education was better than none. What began during a global lockdown became something that outlasted it. Prince was also a Waterford Kamhlaba UWC of Southern Africa alumnus, a school known for selecting students across conflict zones and economic hardship who show unusual potential and commitment. headline_hi: ऑटिज्म से जूझ रहे युवाओं का सहारा
headline_en: Support for youth living with autism
summary_en: A special place has been created in Montana, America, for adults living with autism. It is known as Erik's Ranch & Retreats. It was started by Kathryn Nordberg for the future of her son, Erik. This beautiful farm spans across two hundred and thirty acres of land. Horseback riding and trekking are offered to visiting tourists. All these operations are managed by young people with autism. They work here as guides, cooks, and tour leaders. They receive full wages and accommodation for their hard work. Here, they are learning to lead an independent life with confidence. This farm is bringing a huge change to the lives of these young people.

lead.title: The Montana Ranch Where Autistic People Are Wranglers and Guides
lead.summary: T he staff at Erik’s Ranch & Retreats has a saying: Sheets, towels and lives changed daily .   Erik’s Ranch is a guest retreat where autistic people are concierges, guides, wranglers, cooks and more. Located on 230 acres of pristine pasture and wilderness near Livingston, Montana, the ranch is less than an hour from Yellowstone National Park. It offers horseback riding, fly fishing, nature hikes, history walks and experiences with ranch animals and wildlife — most led or assisted by paid neurodivergent “members,” most of whom also live on the property. The inspiration for Erik’s Ranch dates back to 2008, when founder Kathryn Nordberg was pondering how her son, Erik, whom she described as “a moderately functioning teenager with autism,” would live as an adult — and particularly what would happen when she was no longer around. Ranch manager Cameron Porter (in black hat) and member John Rekedal help a visitor from New Jersey mount her steed for a trail ride. Credit: Jodi Hausen “As someone challenged with expressive language, there weren’t very many opportunities for kids like him,” she said, sitting in the well-appointed kitchen of the ranch’s six-bedroom lodge. So she established a nonprofit with a boutique-style hotel in Edina, Minnesota, where, even after she’s gone, Erik and others like him can live, work and thrive. There, adults on the autism spectrum work and live independently and are guided by life coaches toward achieving personal goals like interviewing, equine or cooking skills; or setting up an Etsy page to sell their artwork. headline_en: New plant generating electricity from air
summary_en: Big news regarding clean energy has emerged from western China. The world's largest liquid-air energy storage plant has begun operations there. This plant is a new way to store green energy for long periods. In this process, clean electricity is used to cool air under extreme pressure. The pressure is so high that the air turns into liquid form. When needed, this liquid air is released rapidly. This spins turbines and generates affordable electricity. This method is considered extremely safe for the environment and cost-effective. It will help prevent the wastage of renewable energy. This project is a major step toward providing the world with clean power.

lead.title: China Switches on World’s Biggest Example of New, Cheap Green Energy Storage
lead.summary: The world’s largest demonstration plant for a new kind of renewable energy storage is up and running in the west of the China. Called liquid-air energy storage (LAES) the plant uses renewable electricity to compress air to extreme densities until it turns to liquid. headline_hi: काई से सजी शहरों की दीवारें
summary_en: In the city of Aachen, Germany, a unique initiative began in the year twenty-twelve. Artist Philipp Wallisfurth wanted to save a one hundred and fifty-year-old tree. Instead of spray paint, he used natural moss. With the help of yogurt, he wrote a message of greenery on a construction wall. People really loved this living art grown on walls. Following this, Philipp developed a new technique to create bio-graffiti using moss. In Cologne as well, he decorated an eight-meter wall with moss. Philipp now lives in Berlin and does this work in several countries. He is turning lifeless concrete walls into lush green art. His art is bringing cities closer to nature.

lead.title: Imagining the Mossy Cities of the Future
lead.summary: This story has been co-published by Reasons to be Cheerful and the Outrider Foundation . I n 2012, Philip Wallisfurth wanted to save a tree. Citizens in Aachen, Germany, were protesting plans for a shopping center that threatened a 150-year-old tree. Wallisfurth , then an aspiring street artist, wondered if he could use moss — instead of his usual spray can — to support the campaign. He harvested moss from a local park, used yogurt as an adhesive and stuck two-meter-high letters onto the construction fence, spelling out “greener living.” The reactions surprised him. “People loved it,” he recalls. “Many took pictures and some spontaneously hung flowers in small vases onto the fence.” He had stumbled upon a medium that was soft, tactile and alive — and a natural way of occupying public space. YouTube tutorials suggested mixing moss with buttermilk in a blender, but the results disappointed him. Through trial and error with different mosses and yogurts, he developed his own approach to making “bio-graffiti.” Artist Philip Wallisfurth developed his own approach to making “bio-graffiti with moss.” Courtesy of Philip Wallisfurth Two years later, whiskey maker Jack Daniel’s hired him for a campaign. In Cologne, Wallisfurth covered an eight-by-eight-meter wall with moss lettering, spelling out a motto he lives by: never give up trying to do what you really want to be happy Now an artist with international projects and a studio in Berlin, Wallisfurth, 42, mostly paints large, colorful murals and designs anamorphic installations, room-filling works that seem to change shape depending on the viewer’s perspective. headline_hi: सर्पगंधा से ब्लड प्रेशर का इलाज
summary_en: In the year nineteen forty-nine, treating high blood pressure was very difficult. There were no definitive medicines to protect patients' hearts and blood vessels. At KEM Hospital in Bombay, Dr. Rustom Jal Vakil worked on this. He began in-depth research on the traditional Indian plant Sarpagandha. The roots of this plant had been used in India for centuries. Dr. Vakil studied it closely on his patients for ten years. He proved that Sarpagandha could safely lower blood pressure. His hard work earned the Indian herb a place in modern medical science. This discovery opened a new path for treating millions of patients worldwide. Even today, this research is considered a great milestone in the Indian medical world.

lead.title: In 1949, This Bombay Doctor Showed How an Indian Plant Could Lower High BP
lead.summary: In the late 1940s, a diagnosis of high blood pressure could leave a patient with few reliable treatment options. Doctors knew hypertension could damage the heart and blood vessels, but finding a medicine that consistently lowered blood pressure remained a formidable challenge.  Among the remedies being tried were sedatives and an assortment of drugs whose effectiveness was uncertain. In Bombay, now Mumbai, cardiologist Dr Rustom Jal Vakil was investigating a different possibility. At King Edward Memorial Hospital, he turned his attention to Rauwolfia serpentina, a plant whose roots had been used in Indian traditional medicine for centuries. Its potential was not entirely unknown in India, but its value had yet to gain widespread acceptance in Western medicine. Vakil's research would help change that. The plant doctors had overlooked The plant, also known as sarpagandha, had a long history in Indian medicine. Its roots had been used for a range of ailments, including snakebites, fever and mental distress. But traditional use alone could not establish whether it was effective against hypertension , or how safely it could be used.   Known as sarpagandha, Rauwolfia serpentina had been used in Indian traditional medicine for centuries to treat various ailments. Photograph: (Amazon)   Vakil approached the question as a clinician and researcher. After returning to India in 1938, following medical training in London, he built a practice around heart disease. He began systematically collecting clinical observations from patients treated with Rauwolfia, examining whether their blood pressure fell and whether the treatment was tolerable.
